advanced_imaging.impression: Abnormal: bilaterally reduced putaminal dopamine transporter uptake, more marked on the left, consistent with a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit.

findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. Age-related cerebral involutional change.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
Mild aortic valve sclerosis without stenosis. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.
echo.impression: Normal biventricular size and systolic function. Mild aortic valve sclerosis without stenosis.

citations: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190
action_criteria.expected_evidence: Entraining, distractible 8-10 Hz left tremor and dragging left leg; right-sided parkinsonism unchanged; symmetric reflexes
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: The examination separates the new left-sided symptoms from her Parkinson's disease: entrainment and distractibility of the tremor and a dragging gait are positive functional signs, while a parkinsonian spread would add rest tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct, mass or other lesion in the right hemisphere or basal ganglia
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI for a new hemibody deficit
action_criteria.rationale: A new left arm weakness in a 61-year-old raises a right hemisphere lesion; one non-contrast MRI with DWI answers it. No gadolinium is needed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interacting pair; venlafaxine listed as a possible tremor contributor
action_criteria.label: Medication review
action_criteria.rationale: Venlafaxine can cause an action tremor, which the review can name; no interaction among her medicines changes the plan.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of comorbid mood, anxiety and somatic symptom burden to guide therapy; no bearing on the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of mood, anxiety and dissociation
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can characterise the comorbidity that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only; the diagnosis and plan for this patient do not depend on a literature result
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on functional neurological disorder
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on positive diagnosis and treatment can inform the explanation and the referral; no step of the diagnostic work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET, DaTscan).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
Increase dopaminergic medication for the functional tremor.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional left tremor and left arm weakness coexisting with Parkinson's disease) based on tremor entrainment and distractibility and a dragging left monoplegic gait, with unchanged parkinsonian signs, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information. Include support for her role as carer for her husband (social work, carer services).
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid depression, with support for her anticipatory grief.

avoided_actions.rationale: No syncope, palpitations or abnormal vital signs; an ECG answers no question raised by a tremor and arm weakness.
The deficit developed over 4 weeks with positive functional signs; there is no embolic question for echocardiography.
There are no episodes of altered awareness or syncope to correlate with a rhythm.
A non-contrast MRI with DWI answers the lesion question; a CT adds radiation and less information.
Nothing suggests inflammation or infection; a lumbar puncture is invasive and answers no question.
The weakness has positive functional signs and normal reflexes; EMG and nerve conduction studies answer no question and a normal result reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Sensation is normal; evoked potentials have no question to answer.
Her Parkinson's disease is established: a DaTscan will be abnormal and cannot distinguish a functional tremor from progression, which the examination does.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder — functional left tremor and left arm weakness superimposed on established right-predominant Parkinson's disease (mixed organic PD + FND)

differential.diagnosis: Progression of Parkinson's disease to the left side
differential.key_features: Spread to the left would add a 4-6 Hz rest tremor with rigidity and bradykinesia; the new tremor is 8-10 Hz, action-predominant, entrains and stops with distraction, and weakness is not a parkinsonian sign.

differential.diagnosis: Right hemisphere stroke or other structural lesion
differential.key_features: Onset over 4 weeks, positive functional signs, symmetric reflexes without a Babinski sign, and no infarct or lesion on MRI with DWI.
Venlafaxine can cause an action tremor, but a drug tremor is bilateral and does not entrain or stop with distraction; hers is left-sided and does both.

key_clinical_evidence: New left 8-10 Hz action-predominant tremor that entrains to an imposed rhythm and is suppressed by distraction, apparent left arm ataxia that resolves with distraction, and a dragging left leg.
Her right-predominant parkinsonism (4 Hz rest tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity) is unchanged; reflexes are symmetric with no Babinski sign.
Non-contrast MRI with DWI shows no lesion to account for the left-sided symptoms.
Functional symptoms commonly coexist with Parkinson's disease; the new symptoms are not progression and do not call for more dopaminergic treatment.
Onset while caring for her terminally ill husband is context, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The new tremor has the features of a functional tremor (frequency, action predominance, entrainment, distractibility); PD and FND coexist.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attributing the new left-sided tremor to disease progression and increasing levodopa or pramipexole, or ordering a DaTscan

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND; it is a treatment target, and the diagnosis rests on the positive signs.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a psychological label without positive signs, or dismissing the symptoms because she is depressed

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive signs; a new hemibody deficit at 61 still warrants one MRI.
red_herrings.data_point: Onset after her husband's diagnosis of terminal lung cancer
red_herrings.intended_effect: Concluding that stress caused the symptoms and skipping the examination for positive signs and the MRI

sequence_constraints.reason: The examination comes first: its positive signs decide whether imaging has a specific question to answer (Espay 2018).

findings.result: The 8-10 Hz action-predominant left hand tremor takes on the frequency of a rhythm imposed by the examiner.
The left hand tremor is suppressed by distracting tasks, and the apparent left arm ataxia resolves with distraction.
The left leg is dragged, added to her baseline right-predominant parkinsonian shuffle.
3/5 on direct testing; reflexes symmetric 2+, no Babinski sign.
Right-predominant bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity and 4 Hz right-hand rest tremor, unchanged.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional tremor and weakness: tremor entrainment, distractibility and a dragging left monoplegic gait. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion; the right-predominant parkinsonian signs are unchanged.

general.proposed: Carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 mg four times daily; Pramipexole 1.0 mg three times daily; Venlafaxine 75 mg once daily
general.summary: No clinically significant interactions among the current medicines. Venlafaxine can cause tremor; pramipexole causes somnolence and impulse control disorders.
warnings: Venlafaxine: postural and action tremor is a recognised adverse effect.
Pramipexole: somnolence and sudden sleep onset; impulse control disorders, dose-related.
Carbidopa/levodopa: no interaction with the other listed medicines.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Review and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder from motor signs of high specificity, and physiotherapy whose effect on the trial's primary outcome was modest; a later revision of the diagnosis is uncommon.

additional_observations: Technique: T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI/ADC and SWI without intravenous contrast. No prior MRI for comparison.
No restricted diffusion. No acute or subacute infarct.
No mass, hemorrhage or white matter lesion in either hemisphere; no lesion in the right corticospinal tract or basal ganglia.
Mild generalized volume loss, appropriate for age.
mri.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No lesion to account for left-sided symptoms. Mild age-appropriate volume loss.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: A new hemibody tremor and weakness in established Parkinson's disease: the agent must tell a functional overlay from progression and stroke on examination, obtain one MRI, and avoid escalating dopaminergic treatment or ordering a DaTscan.
metadata.notes: Functional left tremor and arm weakness superimposed on right-predominant Parkinson's disease; MRI without a lesion.

patient.chief_complaint: New left-sided tremor and weakness — developed over 4 weeks

past_medical_history: Parkinson's disease (diagnosed 6 years ago, on levodopa/carbidopa)

social_history.recent_stressor: Husband diagnosed with terminal lung cancer 3 months ago — caregiver burden; anticipatory grief; change in role from patient to caregiver

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Q is a 61-year-old retired accountant with Parkinson's disease diagnosed 6 years ago (right-sided onset, on carbidopa/levodopa and pramipexole, stable for 2 years) who presents with a 4-week history of a new left-sided tremor and left arm weakness. Her Parkinson's disease has been right-predominant since diagnosis, with a satisfactory response to medication. The left-sided symptoms began about 2 months after her husband was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer and developed over 4 weeks; she now provides full care for him while managing her own Parkinson's disease. She says the new tremor is unlike her right-hand tremor: it is faster, comes on when she uses the hand rather than at rest, and lessens when she is absorbed in a task. She has also noticed that she drags her left leg.

neurological_exam.additional: Known right-predominant Parkinson's disease at baseline. The new findings are on the left side: an 8-10 Hz action tremor that entrains and is distractible, new left arm weakness, and left leg dragging, all developing acutely over 4 weeks.
neurological_exam.coordination: Mild right finger-nose imprecision (PD baseline). Left arm: new apparent ataxia that is variable and resolves with distraction.
neurological_exam.gait: Baseline PD gait (mild right-sided Parkinsonian shuffle, reduced right arm swing). New: left leg dragging added.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Tearful when discussing her husband. MoCA 26/30.
neurological_exam.motor: Baseline PD: mild right-predominant bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity with a 4 Hz right-hand rest tremor. New: left hand now shows a tremor at 8-10 Hz, active and action-predominant, suppressed with distraction, that entrains to an examiner-imposed rhythm. New left arm weakness 3/5.
